questions.prompt: Why did Griffith need his first three injections (live S, live R, heat-killed S) before the mixture result meant anything?

options.text: They showed that mice resist pneumonia after one injection, so the final mouse had to be a new, untreated animal
They showed live S kills, live R is harmless, and dead S alone is harmless — so a death from the mixture had to come from something passing from dead S into live R
They showed that the capsule is made of DNA, so the mixture could be used to measure how much DNA the S cells contained
They showed that heat makes R cells pathogenic, so the mixture death came from the heating step rather than from the S cells

questions.explanation: The controls ruled out each ingredient alone. Only the mixture killed — and the dead mouse was full of living S cells.

questions.prompt: If PROTEIN had been the genetic material, what results would Avery have expected from his two enzyme trials?

options.text: Protease added: mouse lives. DNase added: mouse dies.
Both trials: mouse dies, since the enzymes can't enter the S cells.
Both trials: mouse lives, since both enzymes destroy the capsule.
Protease added: mouse dies. DNase added: mouse lives.

questions.explanation: Destroying the true genetic material should block transformation. Avery actually saw the reverse (protease → dies, DNase → lives), pointing to DNA.

questions.prompt: The lecture compares DNA to a house key. Which two jobs of genetic material does the key represent?

options.text: Its metal stands for the sugar-phosphate backbone, and its teeth stand for the hydrogen bonds between strands
Its shape stands for the capsule, and unlocking a door stands for transformation in Griffith's experiment
Its grooves stand for stored information, and the puzzle of a key copying itself stands for replication with great accuracy
Its grooves stand for the double helix, and turning it in a lock stands for gyrase uncoiling the DNA

questions.explanation: DNA must (1) copy itself with great fidelity and (2) encode genetic information — the key's grooves are encoded information.

questions.prompt: The lecture describes bacterial DNA as 'two rubber bands braided together' and eukaryotic DNA as 'two shoelaces braided together.' What does the comparison capture, along with the matching chromosome count?

options.text: Bacterial DNA is single-stranded and stretchy; eukaryotic DNA is double-stranded and stiff, with a single chromosome in each case
Bacterial DNA is linear with many chromosomes; eukaryotic DNA is circular with one chromosome inside the nucleus
Both are circular, but bacterial loops are smaller, so bacteria have more chromosomes than eukaryotes
Bacterial DNA is double-stranded and circular with a single chromosome; eukaryotic DNA is double-stranded and linear with multiple chromosomes

questions.explanation: Rubber bands = closed loops (circular); shoelaces = ends (linear). Bacteria typically have one chromosome; humans have 46.

questions.prompt: Which two enzymes does the LAGGING strand need over and over, while the leading strand needs them only once or not at all?

options.text: Helicase (to restart the fork) and DNA polymerase (which only works on the lagging strand)
Primase (a new primer for each fragment) and ligase (to glue the Okazaki fragments together)
Gyrase (to supercoil each fragment) and primase (to remove the RNA primers)
Gyrase (to uncoil each fragment) and helicase (to unzip each fragment separately)

questions.explanation: The lagging strand is built in Okazaki fragments, each starting from a new RNA primer and later joined by ligase. The leading strand is one continuous piece.

questions.prompt: How does a bacterium copy one of its plasmids?

options.text: By cutting the plasmid open with ligase so it becomes linear like eukaryotic DNA, then copying it from each free end inward
By transcribing the plasmid into RNA and then copying that RNA back into DNA, because plasmids are too small for helicase to bind
By building one continuous leading strand all the way around the loop from a single primer, since a circle has no lagging strand
The same way it copies its chromosome — starting at an origin where helicases bind, with two replication forks moving in opposite directions around the loop

questions.explanation: Lecture: 'this is also how plasmids get copied' — origin, two helicases, two forks.

questions.prompt: Cipro stops a bacterial population from doubling. Which explanation links its target to the generation time?

options.text: It inhibits DNA polymerase in both bacteria and humans, which is why it is only given in small doses that slow, rather than stop, bacterial growth
It inhibits ligase, so the cell can't seal its membrane during binary fission — the chromosome is copied normally, but splitting fails and the cell bursts
It inhibits gyrase, so the supercoiled chromosome can't be uncoiled and copied — and copying the chromosome is most of the generation time and must happen before binary fission
It inhibits helicase, so the two finished chromosomes stay zipped together and can't be separated into the two daughter cells at division

questions.explanation: Cipro inhibits bacterial gyrase → no uncoiling → no replication → no division. Replication takes most of the ~30-minute generation time.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what would happen if E. coli's DNA polymerase were put into a human cell?

options.text: It would not work at all, because DNA polymerase is the one enzyme that differs between bacteria and humans
It would only work on the lagging strand, because human cells build their leading strand with gyrase
It would build DNA just fine, adding nucleotides complementary to the human DNA, because polymerase is fairly interchangeable between species
It would build bacterial DNA sequences instead of human ones, because the enzyme carries E. coli's genes with it

questions.explanation: Ligase, polymerase, primase, and helicase are pretty interchangeable. Gyrase is the one that is not.

questions.prompt: Why does Craig Venter say he did NOT create artificial life with Mycoplasma genitalium?

options.text: He built the chromosome from the human genome he had helped sequence, so the result was a human-bacterial hybrid, not new life
He built and inserted the 'software' (a synthetic chromosome), but still relied on the existing cell's membrane, ribosomes, and other machinery
He only sequenced the 521 genes and never synthesized a new chromosome, so nothing artificial was ever put into the cell
The synthetic chromosome never worked, so the cell only survived because some of its original chromosome had been left inside

questions.explanation: Venter's view: he provided the programming but used a cell that already had its membrane and ribosomes. He is now trying to build a whole cell.

questions.prompt: What does the 'deoxy' in deoxyribose refer to?

options.text: One carbon of the sugar has just an H where ribose has an OH — the sugar is 'without' that oxygen atom
The sugar has no phosphate group attached, so it can't join the backbone
The sugar contains four carbons instead of the five found in ribose
The sugar has lost its nitrogenous base, so it can't pair with another strand

questions.explanation: Deoxyribose is a 5-carbon sugar like ribose, minus one oxygen (H instead of OH).

questions.prompt: Since primase and DNA polymerase can only build in the 5'→3' direction, to which end of a growing strand is each new nucleotide added?

options.text: The 3' end, which finishes with an OH group
The 5' end, which begins with a phosphate group
Either end, depending on which strand is the template
The middle of the strand, where the replication fork opens

questions.explanation: A strand runs from a 5' phosphate to a 3' OH. Building 5'→3' means each new nucleotide is added at the 3' OH end.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the DNA replication enzymes is FALSE?

options.text: Helicase unzips and unwinds the double helix, forming a replication fork.
Primase builds a short primer out of DNA nucleotides.
Gyrase removes the supercoiling from the chromosome.
Ligase glues Okazaki fragments together.
DNA polymerase extends the new strand and later replaces the primer with DNA.

questions.explanation: False — the primer is made of RNA, not DNA.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the history of DNA discovery is FALSE?

options.text: After Griffith's mixture killed the mouse, its body held only living R cells.
The 1962 Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins.
Avery's protease/DNase experiment was done in 1944.
Griffith's experiment was done in 1928.
Hershey and Chase confirmed in 1952 that DNA is the genetic material.

questions.explanation: False — the dead mouse was swarming with living S cells, even though no living S cells had been injected.

questions.prompt: Explain how three features of DNA's structure — complementary base pairing, hydrogen bonds between strands, and antiparallel strands — each matter for replication.
questions.explanation: Complementary base pairing (A–T, G–C) means each strand carries the information to rebuild the other, so replication is accurate: separate the strands and add the matching nucleotides, giving two identical molecules (each with one old and one new strand — semi-conservative). Hydrogen bonds between the bases are weak enough for helicase to unzip the strands into a replication fork, while the covalent sugar-phosphate backbone keeps each strand intact. Antiparallel strands run in opposite directions, and since primase and polymerase only build 5'→3', one daughter strand (leading) is built continuously toward the fork while the other (lagging) is built away from it in Okazaki fragments that ligase joins.

questions.prompt: Using E. coli, explain the difference between genotype and phenotype and how a gene connects the two.
questions.explanation: Genotype is the genes and other nucleotide sequences in the genome — the order of A, G, C, and T. Phenotype is the physical, behavioral, and metabolic traits that result, such as E. coli's rod shape, being Gram-negative, and being a facultative anaerobe. A gene is a region of the chromosome that encodes the primary structure (amino acid order) of a specific protein; the proteins a cell makes carry out its functions and build its structures, so the genotype determines the phenotype. E. coli has about 5,000 genes.
